↳ Posted by gian marco on January 25th, 2003.

I think this is one of those tonally ambivalent tunes that people can argue about for ever! There are plenty of them in ITM.
I base my argument for Emin mainly on the fact that every fourth bar, which includes the last bars in the A and B parts, ends in Emin, so it can be said that the tonal trend is clearly towards Emin.
Regarding the 1st, 3rd and 5th bars which give an impression of Gmaj, I think the way in which they start with a strong B3 foreshadows the change to Emin later on in the tune; B, being the 5th of the key of Emin, is the second strongest tonal point in that key, but is not the second strongest tonal point in G. If the tune had G3 instead of B3 in bars 1, 3 and 5 there would have been a stronger impression of Gmaj and I think the transition to Emin would have sounded more abrupt.
Perhaps the easy way to settle this sort of thing would be to define the key of the tune solely by the number of sharps or flats, leaving the player and listener to decide whether it is major, minor or modal. But then we wouldn’t be having these interesting discussions - or would we?

Cucanandy

A well-known guitarist, banjoist and teacher in the NYC Irish scene teaches this tune in 3/4 as a hop jig -- which is DIFFERENT than any other kind of jig and is not done anymore -- he knows about 11 more tunes called hop jigs - they are NOT slip jigs although the bounce of SOME slip jigs can be the same as the hop jig. Somewhere along the line it looks like people haved melded the hop jig into the slip jig simply because they had no info on the hop jig

I’ve never known this tune to be anything but a “hop jig”. It often gets paired with “The Dusty Miller”, another tune of this type. Wouldn’t go so far as to write it out in 3/4 though; it’s definitely in 9/8 with a SLIGHT 3/4 feel to the rhythm. I have it as follows:

↳ Posted by Harald Wellmann on April 17th, 2023.

Cucanandy, X:10 (as “piping style” hop jig)

Whether it’s an old way or a new fad, it’s becoming quite popular to play hop jigs in a fast, straightened-out style – and pipers are leading the charge.

Played that way, tunes have such a different feel that you find yourself tapping your foot “three-one” instead of “one-two-three”. So much so that the big hop jig fans like Caoimhín Ó Raghallaigh are teaching the “special hop jig tap way” in their classes :-D

I actually find it a lot of fun to play them like that, and tapping your foot “three-one” does make a huge difference! The only problem was trying to put down the dots for others so that they don’t look like regular slip jigs instead of fast, no-breaking-at-turns tunes. Then it dawned on me that the pipers et. al. aren’t actually playing them in 9/8, they’re effectively playing them in 3/2.

So here is the three-two version of Cucanandy with an example of “straightened-out” playing by Nathan Gourley, Joey Abarta and Owen Marshall below:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=leBjvIxV_OU&t=96s

(NB: This being a recording of superb musicians from the US, I’ve seen some folks suggest that fast hop jigs are the “American thing” – but I can tell it’s most definitely not, dig a bit deeper and you can find yourself listening to Mick O’Brien or Tiarnán Ó Duinnchinn play endless sets of these tunes if you’re lucky!)

↳ Posted by Jeremy on July 31st, 2026.

Re: Cucanandy

Bregolas, I don’t agree that Joey/Nathan/Owen are playing in 3/2 - it’s worth listening to how english musicians actually play 3/2 hornpipes, as it’s quite different. The underlying feel in Joey/Nathan/Owen’s playing is still triplet based (just quite fast, and you wouldn’t typically play every beat with triplets or you’d lose the hop jig feel).

Michael Gorman’s talk and demonstration about the difference between slip and hop jigs is quite informative, and he definitely plays the one type quite rhythmically similarly to them. (Note that he reverses the labels! Also interestingly calls the one we call slip jigs now a group dance…)

↳ Posted by Nico on July 31st, 2026.

Re: Cucanandy

Sure, that was a flawed experiment – but I never suggested they played it as an English three-two hornpipe, that’s definitely not it! This was more about grouping the notes in a measure in a way that would reflect how a hop jig rhythm is strikingly different from that of a slip jig (and Cucanandy can be played as both).

Going back to that fine recording, if you slow it down a lot (for science), you’ll notice it doesn’t really become a slip jig or reveal a slip jig feel – only one beat per measure is audibly accented and one would have to strain to hear any steady triplet rhythm there (at least I don’t). Which is not to say there aren’t other takes on hop jigs different from the “driving” style some pipers like to play them nowadays, maybe somewhere in the middle.

FWIW, I’ve since tried notating hop jigs in 3/4 like others before. I don’t really like how that looks and one could certainly be triggered by such a notation :-) But at least it *sounds* closer to an actual hop jig when played in various ABC software without any custom swing modifications. The defaults for the 9/8 playback are totally incompatible with the hop jig rhythm and feel.

For me, time signature =/= rhythm, it’s a matter of conveniently grouping the notes that makes sense for the melody. Unfortunately, in reality every meter comes loaded with certain associations and expectations of rhythm – so every choice for outliers like this becomes merely an approximation. You might say that the jig triplets are implied in hop jigs even when it’s hard to hear them in live performance – but when given a hop jig notated in 9/8 without context, most people would play it as a pronounced slip jig in moderate tempo. Meanwhile, hornpipes can be played with a strong triplety swing but you’ll have hard time finding one notated in 12/8 today even though some musicians *do* believe that it’s the “proper” time signature for them (it may technically be correct when played that way but it also looks odd). Can’t win either way!

I guess the way to go about it in ABC is to follow the convention of 6/8 – 9/8 – 12/8 for any sort of jigs and 4/4 for hornpipes & co., and then keep adding the MIDI swing presets indefinitely depending on the rhythm. Including but not limited to hop jigs, barndances and highlands. I might do just that in my custom fork of ABC Transcription Tools :-D
